title: Adapter Pattern
oneLiner: Wraps an incompatible interface in a translator so two mismatched pieces of code can work together unchanged.

hero.name: The Translator
hero.catchphrase: Speak your language, I'll speak theirs.
hero.power: Wraps an incompatible interface so existing code can call it without ever changing either side.
hero.weakness: Wrap enough mismatched systems and you get a maze of translators — sometimes the real fix is agreeing on one interface, not adapting forever.
hero.origin: The Translator appeared when a shipping module built for a `getRate(weight)` API had to suddenly talk to a legacy carrier whose API only exposed `computeCost(pounds, zone)`.

story.problem: Your app's checkout flow calls `gateway.charge(amount)` everywhere. The new legacy carrier's SDK only exposes `LegacyGateway.submitPayment(cents, currencyCode)` — a completely different shape.
story.solution: The Translator wraps LegacyGateway in a small adapter class that implements the familiar `charge(amount)` interface, converting units and calling the legacy method underneath.
story.result: Checkout code never learns the legacy SDK exists. It keeps calling `charge(amount)`, and the adapter handles the translation invisibly.

before: Checkout code riddled with special-casing for the legacy SDK's shape
Every call site has to know both APIs
Swapping providers means editing business logic
after: Checkout code calls one familiar interface everywhere
Only the adapter knows the legacy SDK's shape
Swapping providers means writing one new adapter

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Checkout code has a special if-branch just to call the legacy carrier's oddly-shaped API.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Our whole checkout flow expects charge(amount). This legacy SDK wants submitPayment(cents, currencyCode). Now what?

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Translator steps between the two systems, headset on.
panels.speaker: The Translator
panels.dialogue: Don't rewrite your checkout flow. I'll stand between them and translate every call.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: A LegacyGatewayAdapter implements the familiar PaymentGateway interface, converting units underneath.
panels.speaker: The Translator
panels.dialogue: Call charge(amount) like always. I'll convert it to cents and call submitPayment() for you.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: Checkout code is unchanged. Only one new adapter file exists.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Zero changes to checkout logic. We just plugged in a translator and it worked.

useWhen: You need to use an existing class whose interface doesn't match what your code expects, and you can't change either side.
You're integrating a third-party or legacy library and want to isolate its quirks behind a clean interface.
You want to introduce a new implementation of an interface without touching any existing callers.
avoidWhen: You control both interfaces — just make them match instead of adapting forever.
You'd need to adapt so many mismatched methods that the adapter becomes as complex as a rewrite.
The 'mismatch' is trivial (a renamed parameter) and doesn't justify a whole extra class.
commonMistakes: Writing adapters for every third-party call instead of consolidating behind one clean boundary, leading to adapter sprawl.
Letting adapter-specific quirks (like unit conversion bugs) go untested, since the adapter is 'just plumbing'.
Adapting an interface so loosely that subtle behavior differences (error codes, edge cases) leak through unnoticed.
Confusing Adapter (make incompatible interfaces work together) with Decorator (add behavior to a compatible interface).
explanation.realWorldExample: Database driver wrappers that expose a uniform query interface over different vendors, `.forEach` polyfills adapting array-likes to real arrays, and payment SDK wrappers unifying multiple providers behind one interface are all Adapter.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this the same as Facade? Both hide something behind a simpler interface.

conversation.speaker: The Translator
conversation.message: Close cousins, different jobs. Facade simplifies a subsystem that was ALREADY compatible in spirit. I make two genuinely incompatible interfaces work together.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When do I stop writing new adapters?

conversation.speaker: The Translator
conversation.message: When you're adapting the same system in five different places — that's a sign to consolidate into one shared adapter instead of five one-off ones.

codeBattle.scenario: Your app supports Stripe today. Tomorrow you need Razorpay and PayPal. Each provider has a different API.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Translator lets each provider's mismatched API be wrapped into one common interface your checkout code already expects, without changing the original implementations.

quiz.question: What problem does Adapter solve?
options: Two interfaces are incompatible and neither can be changed to match the other
An object needs to be cloned instead of constructed
A class needs exactly one instance
A complex subsystem needs a simpler interface
quiz.answer: Two interfaces are incompatible and neither can be changed to match the other
quiz.explanation: Adapter's entire purpose is bridging a mismatch you can't fix at the source.

quiz.question: How does an Adapter typically work internally?
options: It wraps the incompatible object and translates calls to match the expected interface
It rewrites the incompatible class's source code
It deletes the incompatible interface and replaces it globally
It merges both interfaces into a single new class permanently
quiz.answer: It wraps the incompatible object and translates calls to match the expected interface
quiz.explanation: The adapter holds a reference to the wrapped object and converts each call's shape on the way through.

quiz.question: What's the key difference between Adapter and Facade?
options: Adapter bridges incompatible interfaces; Facade simplifies access to an already-usable subsystem
They are the exact same pattern with different names
Facade only works with legacy code, Adapter only works with new code
Adapter requires a database, Facade does not
quiz.answer: Adapter bridges incompatible interfaces; Facade simplifies access to an already-usable subsystem
quiz.explanation: Facade is about hiding complexity in a compatible subsystem; Adapter is about resolving genuine incompatibility.

quiz.question: What's a sign you're overusing the Adapter pattern?
options: You've written many one-off adapters for the same system instead of consolidating behind one boundary
You have exactly one adapter for one legacy dependency
Your adapter implements a well-defined interface
quiz.answer: You've written many one-off adapters for the same system instead of consolidating behind one boundary
quiz.explanation: Adapter sprawl around the same dependency usually means it's time to unify behind one clean wrapper.
